doc.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996

title: Jazz as international and versatile
summary: Jazz has spread worldwide; musicians must play Latin, funk, classical and more, and younger players do it naturally.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: play. They can really play. You can not say that jazz is American anymore. Jazz started in America, particularly by black people. But now it has spread throughout the world and has become a proven formula. And it’s transcended all racial, sexual and religious nationalistic lines, that if you submit to the music, you will have success, and be able to get to what you’re saying inside. Because now there are young kids from other countries that understand what this music is about. So now, when me and my generations that are coming behind me, when we go to Europe, we have to keep our eyes open because we’re not special, as in terms of we’re not rare birds, because Hans may come over here and he may blow some stuff that will blow you away. So it ain’t about just being American and blowing your horn and you ain’t going to have any competition, because you’ve got guys coming out of the woodwork all over the world. So what I’m trying to say is where the music is going is it’s taking on the international stage. And that means that the jazz musician has an obligation to bring all kinds of things into his jazz. So I feel that the jazz musicians that are going to be important in years to come are going to be the ones that give you a variety of colors, a variety of sounds, who are able to do a variety of musics, not just swinging anymore. Because we’ve got the Latin, the Latino stuff is very strong, the Cubans are coming here now, very strong. So in the past there were good players in the rhythm section that could play good jazz, good bebop, but couldn’t give it the Latin thing. And then you started to have jazz guys that were starting to realize that bass players, that hey, you’ve got to go [scats] and get into that and learn clave, and you started to get this crossover as they call it or fusion as they call it. What do they mean by that? You know what I mean? It’s just the world is getting smaller and people are able to travel you know, and travel is cheaper, so you have a thing that all cultures have this level of virtuosity in their culture. So as a jazz musician, and Art used to say as a jazz musician, it’s the highest form of our musical instrument, I’m not going to back down from any type of music. Because I’m a jazz man, and I’m supposed to be able to play anything. So it’s up to me to get with it. So I feel that this is the mindset for the future, is that you should be able to swing and play the bop, but you also should be able to jump in there with some salsa and jump in there with some funk, play – read your ass off, and play some classical music you know, and play some show tunes, play some dinner music, I do weddings you know? I try to do it all. And that’s what you see is the difference between the older guys and the younger guys. The younger guys can play everything. They’re into James Brown. It’s not just a superficial — oh I’m going to play some funk let’s put a back beat on it, like when the older cats maybe try to crossover. And that’s only because of a generational thing you know. And you have to keep your eyes on the youth and what’s coming behind you and take that and incorporate it.
